job.title: Allstate Agency Owner - CEO of You

realStack: Allstate Exclusive Agency platform (agency management system / book-of-business administration)
Allstate sales tools and product-quoting systems for Property & Casualty and Life & Health policies
State licensing credentials — Property & Casualty and Life & Health (regulatory prerequisite)
Small-business financial tooling: budgeting, payroll, lease/utilities and operating-expense management
Allstate training, incentive and bonus/commission programs
The Exclusive Agency Agreement and Exclusive Agency Program materials (the contract governing the role)
coreResponsibilities: Own and operate an Allstate exclusive insurance agency as an independent contractor, with full P&L responsibility
Sell and cross-sell Allstate P&C and Life & Health products; educate prospects and convert them to customers
Generate new business through networking, prospecting and trust-building in the local community
Grow and retain a book of business, earning recurring revenue from policy renewals
Recruit, hire, empower and manage agency staff and build a collaborative agency culture
Run day-to-day operations — budgeting, planning, staffing, marketing and expense control
Invest and manage liquid startup capital to fund payroll, lease, marketing and operating costs
Leverage Allstate's brand, tools and resources to drive growth and hit commission/bonus targets
statedVsRealGaps: roleFamily is tagged 'marketing,' but the real role is insurance SALES plus small-business owner-operator management; marketing is only one of several resources Allstate supplies, not the job's core.
seniorityTarget 'medior' understates reality — this is an owner/GM-level position carrying P&L, staffing and capital responsibility, not a mid-level employee role.

Framed as a salaried-sounding 'need,' but it is NOT employment: agents are exclusive-agent independent contractors bound by the Allstate Exclusive Agency Agreement. The 'be your own boss / CEO of You' autonomy is real on operations but constrained to selling Allstate products only.

'No franchise or royalty fees' is emphasized, yet the role still requires a substantial liquid-capital investment to cover payroll, lease, marketing and utilities — the financial risk sits with the owner.

'Previous insurance experience not required' coexists with a hard requirement to obtain state P&C and Life & Health licenses before appointment — a real regulatory barrier, not an optional nice-to-have.
Earnings are 'control your earnings potential' commission/bonus, i.e. variable and at-risk income, not a fixed salary the 'need' framing implies.

Stated stack and responsibilities arrays were empty; both had to be reconstructed from the JD, and the JD is recruitment-marketing copy with key figures (years in business, capital amount) redacted — no concrete quotas or day-to-day metrics are given.
riskAreas: Capital risk: meaningful personal liquid-capital exposure to stand up and run the agency, despite the 'no fees' messaging.
Regulatory/licensing gate: must secure P&C and Life & Health licenses across applicable states before appointment.
Misaligned classification in the need record (marketing/medior) vs. the actual entrepreneurial sales-and-ownership profile — would mis-route sourcing and screening.
Income variability and ramp risk: commission/renewal-driven earnings depend on building a book from scratch.
Constrained independence: 'own your business' but exclusive-agent status limits product lines to Allstate; success is tied to one carrier's competitiveness and program terms.
Candidate-fit risk: the role rewards a proactive, capitalized, sales-driven self-starter with management appetite — quite different from a typical marketing hire.
analysis.reflection: This is recruitment-marketing copy for an Allstate exclusive-agency ownership opportunity, not a conventional salaried marketing role, and there is no codebase to reflect against — appropriately so for an insurance-sales/business-ownership function. Reflected against its own materials, the real 'body of work' is a local insurance agency: a P&C and Life & Health book of business run on Allstate's agency-management, lead-gen, sales and CRM tooling, under the Exclusive Agency Agreement. The honest divergence is between the need record's labels (roleFamily 'marketing,' seniority 'medior,' empty stack) and what the JD actually describes: a licensed, capitalized owner-operator who sells, staffs, budgets and grows an agency as an independent contractor with variable, renewal-driven income. Judged in the role's own terms — full P&L ownership, two-line licensing, hiring and managing staff, and personal capital at risk — the true complexity is high, even though Allstate supplies substantial scaffolding. The biggest screening risks are treating it as a mid-level marketing employee role and underweighting the capital, licensing and sales-ownership demands.

case.title: Stand up the Westerville, OH Allstate Exclusive Agency — first-year build plan
case.brief: You are the prospective owner of a brand-new Allstate Exclusive Agency in Westerville, Ohio (a Columbus suburb). Allstate has assigned you a small starter book and given you access to its lead, quoting and agency-management tools; the rest — capital, staffing, market, P&L — is yours to run as an independent contractor. This is a sales-and-ownership work sample, not a marketing campaign: you act on a book of business, a capital model, a commission schedule and the Exclusive Agency Agreement the way an agency owner would, producing the artifacts you'd actually take into a launch decision. The materials handed to you are deliberately realistic and partly incomplete — that mirrors the real role, where the Allstate program documents answer some questions and leave others to your judgment. Use insurance-agency language throughout (households, policies, lines, premium, renewals, quote→bind, book, producer/CSR, P&L). You have a hard cap of ~2 hours, so depth beats coverage: make the few high-leverage calls well rather than producing many thin documents. Polished spreadsheets and prose are assumed to be tool-assisted; what we evaluate is the judgment underneath — which is why one deliverable is a short DECISIONS log, kept the way any operator keeps notes on the calls they had to make.
case.repoSeed:
A folder of starting materials representative of a new Allstate Exclusive Agency, not software:
- starter_book.csv — the assigned/transferred book (~110 households, ~180 active policies). Columns: household_id, primary_named_insured, city, lines_active, auto_term (6mo|12mo), home_term, annual_premium, renewal_date, tenure_years, multiline_flag (Y/N), last_rate_change_pct. A meaningful share are monoline auto with multiline_flag=N (cross-sell candidates); several renewals fall in the next 90 days; a cluster carries last_rate_change_pct ≥ 12 (at-risk after a rate action).
- crm_export.csv — current open pipeline and the upcoming renewals, with status, stage, last_contact_date and at-risk flags.
- lead_lists/allstate_provided_leads.csv — vendor/Allstate-supplied leads (volume high, intent mixed). lead_lists/community_targets.csv — a hand-built local list (realtors, small-business owners, a local employer, two HOAs).
- capital_and_operating.xlsx — three tabs: 'Capital' (liquid capital available: $62,500), 'OpEx' (lease $2,400/mo, utilities+tech $900/mo, E&O, owner draw target, marketing line left blank for you), 'Comp Plan' (Allstate base commission + the enhanced-compensation/bonus thresholds, with the bonus gate noted but not fully worked out).
- commission_schedule.pdf — new-business vs renewal commission rates for P&C (auto/home) and Life & Health; new-business rates are higher and paid on bind, renewal rates lower and paid at each policy's renewal; auto is largely 6-month term, home 12-month.
- exclusive_agency_agreement_excerpt.pdf — key clauses from the Exclusive Agency Agreement and program supplement: exclusivity (Allstate-only placement), production/retention expectations, expense responsibility, and the economic-interest / Termination Payment (TPP) treatment of the book.
- market_brief.md — Westerville snapshot: households, median income, owner-occupancy, the incumbent carriers/agencies, and notes on local channels.
tasks: Build a 90-day go-to-market and book-build plan (1–2 pages plus any supporting sheet). Using starter_book.csv, both lead_lists files and market_brief.md, decide where the first 90 days of selling effort go: prioritize prospecting channels, design a multi-line cross-sell play aimed at the monoline households (multiline_flag = N), and set weekly activity targets with the explicit quote→bind conversion assumptions behind them. Include a retention play for the renewals flagged at-risk in crm_export.csv / starter_book.csv (rows with last_rate_change_pct ≥ 12).

Build a 12-month operating P&L and capital plan from capital_and_operating.xlsx (Capital, OpEx, Comp Plan tabs) and commission_schedule.pdf. Show monthly cash, the deepest cash trough (lowest balance and the month it occurs), and the break-even month. Make and defend the staffing call — when, whether, and whom to hire (licensed producer vs lower-cost unlicensed CSR) — and the marketing allocation, both tied to the cash plan. State plainly whether the $62,500 of liquid capital is sufficient and, if not, the cushion you would want before signing.

Read exclusive_agency_agreement_excerpt.pdf and reconcile Tasks 1–2 against it. Produce a short risk register (5–8 rows): for each item give the clause or reality it stems from, its impact on your plan, and your mitigation. At minimum cover the P&C and Life & Health licensing gate and its effect on your realistic start date, and call out anything in your go-to-market or financials that the agreement constrains, limits or contradicts.

Keep a DECISIONS log (½–1 page) alongside the deliverables. For every call you made where the materials were open or silent — how fast you deployed capital/marketing, how you modeled new-business vs renewal commission and policy terms, staffing, and product mix — record what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and the one question you would put to your Allstate Field Sales Leader / territory manager before committing. Frame it as the working notes any operator keeps, not a test answer.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 marketing line on the 'OpEx' tab (left blank) + Task 1 channel choice; the brief gives total capital but no spend pace.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate sizes the cash trough first and pegs marketing/activity to a runway and a ruin constraint; a naive one picks a round marketing number and never connects it to the lowest-cash month or the licensing-delayed start.
decisionSpace: Front-load marketing and paid leads to build the book fast — quicker renewal income later, but a deeper cash trough and higher early-ruin risk on $62,500.
Pace spend to protect runway — safer cash position, slower ramp, more dependence on owner-driven prospecting in the first quarter.

Lean on free/included Allstate leads + community_targets networking first, scaling paid spend only after the first bind cohort proves a conversion rate — lowest burn but channel- and timing-dependent.

coverProbes.where: exclusive_agency_agreement_excerpt.pdf — exclusivity, economic-interest / Termination Payment (TPP), and production clauses (Task 3, and the equity/cross-sell framing in Task 1).
coverProbes.reveals: A candidate who actually reads it discovers the agent does not own the book outright (economic interest + TPP, conditions attached) and is single-carrier by contract; a naive one plans to diversify carriers or treats the book as a freely sellable personal asset and a recruiting 'equity' pitch.
decisionSpace: Treat single-carrier exclusivity as a brand/cost advantage and go all-in on Allstate product depth (P&C + Life cross-sell) rather than carrier breadth.
Acknowledge single-carrier concentration as a real risk and hedge inside the allowed product set (broaden P&C + Life & Health mix, deepen retention) rather than placing outside business.
Build the staffing/equity story honestly around the TPP/economic-interest reality instead of an 'own a sellable book' promise, adjusting how the role is sold to a hired producer.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 P&L using commission_schedule.pdf — new-business vs renewal rates and 6-month auto vs 12-month home terms.
coverProbes.reveals: Distinguishes candidates who model commission by cohort and term (new-business paid on bind, renewal paid lower and only at each policy's renewal) from those whose one-shot model applies a blended rate to all premium from month 1 — which passes a shallow 'does it break even?' check but overstates early income and mis-times the trough.
decisionSpace: Cohort/term-accurate model: separate new-business and renewal streams, respect 6-month auto vs 12-month home renewal timing — most rigorous, slower to build.
Simplified annualized blended commission with the limitation explicitly flagged and a stated correction direction — fast and defensible if the caveat is named.
Conservative renewal-lagged ramp (assume renewals only begin contributing after the first full term, haircut new-business retention) — robust to error but may under-call the upside.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 staffing decision; the materials never specify headcount, only an owner draw target and the licensing prerequisite.
coverProbes.reveals: A good answer ties the hire to the cash plan and the P&C/Life licensing timeline; a naive one asserts a hire (or none) with no link to the cash trough, break-even month, or who can legally bind business before the owner is licensed.
decisionSpace: Hire a licensed producer up front to add selling capacity from day one — accelerates the book but is the heaviest payroll burn against thin early cash.
Start solo and add a producer only after break-even or a proven conversion rate — protects runway, caps early sales throughput.

Hire a lower-cost unlicensed CSR for service/admin while the owner sells, deferring a producer — cheaper and frees owner selling time, but adds no licensed bind capacity and leans on the owner's own license being in place.
